steps.caption: White to move, in check. Only the one rook on d1 can do anything about it.

line.say: The rook takes the checking rook. It is the only move the rules allow, so there was nothing to decide.
Black takes back with the bishop, and the trade is even.

steps.text:
In a timed game every second you spend is a second you do not have later. So the clock works like a **budget**: you can think long about a few moves, or briefly about many, but not long about all of them.
The move you just made cost almost nothing to choose, because the rules left only one. Two other kinds of position come next.

steps.caption: No check and nothing hanging. Four sensible moves are marked, and a chess program rates them all within about half a pawn of each other. A long think will not find a clear winner here. Stockfish 19 (lite), depth 16, my run [V]: d4 +0.32, Bb5 +0.28, Bc4 +0.19, Nc3 +0.15.
Same position. Each good move has its own idea, and choosing between them is a matter of taste more than of danger.

Black asks the bishop a question: stay and be challenged, or retreat?

steps.caption: Another good idea in the same position.

steps.caption: White to move. The queen can take the knight on f6. It looks as if White wins a knight for free.

line.say: The queen takes the knight: three points won, for a moment.
A pawn guarded f6, so it takes the queen. White paid nine points for three.

steps.caption: Same position, a calm move. The queen steps back to a safe square, and the few seconds spent checking who guards f6 have saved it. Stockfish 19 (lite), depth 16 [V]: Qe3 +0.30, O-O +0.30, e5 +0.17.

line.say: The queen retreats out of reach of everything and loses nothing.

steps.text:
A capture can be a gift or a bait. **Rule of thumb:** before you take, count who guards the piece, and compare the values. A queen (counting value 9) taking a knight (3) that a pawn guards loses six points.
This is where the clock should go. Positions with a tempting capture are the ones where a single quick move can lose the game.

steps.title: Where should the time go?
steps.prompt: The three positions differ in side, structure and theme, so ignore those. Name the one feature that sets the clock advice: how many sensible moves exist, and whether a capture is a trap. Then check.

steps.text:
Games are timed with two numbers, like **10+5**. The first is the minutes each player starts with. The second is the *increment*: seconds added to your clock after every move you make. If your clock reaches zero you usually lose, whatever the board shows.
Worked example, 15+10 and 30 moves: 15 minutes is 900 seconds, the increment adds 30 × 10 = 300, total 1,200. Divide by the 30 moves: **40 seconds a move** on average.

steps.prompt: Now you try. Time control 10+5, and you play 40 moves. How many seconds do you have in total, and how many seconds per move on average?

steps.text:
An average hides a problem. [H] Hard decisions tend to arrive late, when the clock is lowest; test that on your own games. So keep a **reserve**, a block of seconds you promise not to touch until the end.
Example, 5+0, reserve 60 seconds, 35 moves: (300 − 60) ÷ 35 is about 6.9 seconds a move. Forced moves cost almost nothing, so they add to what is left for the hard ones. Treat these numbers as a first guess to test, not a law.

steps.prompt: Two more sums. (1) Control 5+0, reserve 60 seconds, 35 moves: average seconds per move, to one decimal? (2) Control 3+2: how many seconds of increment have you gained after 30 moves?

steps.caption: Opening moves you already know well can be played in a few seconds each. Those saved seconds are what pay for the hard moments later.

steps.caption: A look-alike. White is in check, yet White has seven legal moves: four king steps, two blocks and one capture. Check is not the same as forced, so count the legal moves first.

line.say: One of the seven takes the checking rook and wins it. A quick glance would have missed this.

steps.text:
Another look-alike is time trouble. The pattern named after Alexander Kotov, as summarised in a reference article (his book was not read by us): long hesitation over a hard choice, then a hurried move when the clock is nearly empty [S].
With several equal moves and little time, pick one and play.

steps.prompt: Explain to a friend why a forced move should cost almost no clock, and what you do with the seconds you saved. Write two sentences in your own words, then tick what you included.

fields.label: A forced move leaves nothing to decide
The saved seconds go to positions that need a decision

steps.text:
A model answer: when the rules leave one move, thinking cannot improve it, so play it. The seconds saved are a gift to later moves.
[I] Engine-equal does not mean unimportant: choosing a plan in a balanced position is a human decision, so spend saved seconds there. A tempting capture also deserves a count of the guards.

**A routine for any move.** Ask in order: (1) How many legal moves do I have? If one, play it. (2) Is there a check, capture or threat for either side? Count guards and values. (3) If not, pick a plan, choose a sensible move and go.
[I] A habit to practise, not a law. [H] When low on clock, shorten step 3 and choose the simplest safe move; one quick blunder may cost more than many slightly inferior moves. Check it against your lost games.
